# Why did Baldur's Gate 3 get a wave of negative reviews after Patch 7, and what were players angry about?

Between September 1, 2024, and October 31, 2024, about 96.7% of sampled reviews for **Baldur's Gate 3** were positive, meaning only 3.3% of the reviews in this window were negative [R86][R87]. Despite this overwhelmingly positive overall reception, a minor wave of negative reviews followed the release of Patch 7 on September 5, 2024, which introduced official mod support, new evil ending cinematics, split-screen improvements, and Honour Mode updates [R80][R86][R87]. Players who wrote negative reviews were angry that the new official mod manager broke existing game saves, disabled third-party mods, and caused persistent multiplayer connection and synchronization failures [R92][R98][R118].

## Timeline

* **June 2024**: **Baldur's Gate 3** has an average of 58,746 concurrent players and a peak of 103,767 [R75].
* **July 2024**: The game averages 66,694 players, peaking at 115,180 [R76].
* **August 2024**: Player counts remain stable with 66,700 average players and a 119,687 peak [R77].
* **September 5, 2024**: Patch 7 is released on PC, adding official modding support, split-screen improvements, new evil endings, and new Legendary Actions for Honour Mode [R80].
* **September 2024**: Average player counts rise by 9.43% to 72,993, with a peak of 136,574 [R78].
* **September 19, 2024**: Larian releases Hotfix #26 on PC to resolve a game crash and fix a bug where enemies retained Honour Mode Legendary Actions on non-Honour-Mode saves [R81].
* **October 1, 2024**: Patch 7 rolls out to console and Mac alongside Hotfix #27, which addresses modding experience issues [R80][R82].
* **October 16, 2024**: Hotfix #28 is released to fix crashes, blockers, and Mod Manager enable-disable loops during multiplayer [R84].
* **October 2024**: Average players drop by 15.04% to 62,014, with a peak of 120,185 [R79].

## What players say

Out of 600 sampled reviews across English and Simplified Chinese, 580 were positive and 20 were negative [R86][R87]. This indicates that the massive majority of players praised the game and remained highly satisfied during this period [R86][R87]. The negative review share was slightly higher among English players at 4.3% compared to Simplified Chinese players at 2.3% [R86][R87].

However, the critical minority focused heavily on technical issues introduced by the patch [R92][R98][R118]. The primary complaint was that the official mod manager corrupted mod libraries, broke existing save files, and stopped third-party mods from working [R92][R98][R113]. For example, a player with 363.8 hours of playtime complained: "I will change this once they fix their mod manager.  As of right now it breaks the game" [R92]. Another player with 298.8 hours noted: "funny how larians attempt to support mods basically destroyed everyones saves and made mods stop working" [R98].

Additionally, players experienced a bug where the manager would auto-resubscribe and re-download deleted mods, compounded by login loops on the modding website [R97][R99]. Others criticized broken multiplayer lobbies, desyncs, and lack of helpful error messages [R93][R118][R126]. A player with 78.3 hours stated: "My negative review hinges entirely upon terribly buggy and poorly thought out multiplayer. Bought the game to play with friends, and it just constantly has problems playing multiplayer" [R93].

Other complaints included general performance degradation, crashes on high-end PCs, and a frustrating new mechanic in the evil endings where non-Dark Urge players who used tadpoles were forced into a mind flayer transformation unless they passed a difficult DC 25 Constitution save [R94][R123][R127].

## What the data can't answer

The player count data cannot show exact daily correlations with the release of Patch 7 beyond monthly aggregated averages.

Furthermore, standard limits apply: Steam reviews only reflect the opinions of players who write reviews, and this data does not include console player counts. The developers' motives are only known as stated in their official announcements [R80][R81]. Finally, SteamSpy owner estimates were not provided in the findings.

Patch #7 Now Live!

[quote=author]EDIT:

Patch 7 is now rolling out to console and Mac players! This update also brings both Hotfix #26 and now Hotfix #27 to all platforms! Catch up on the latest patch notes here.

Hey gang, 

Are you ready to embrace evil? Do you yearn to see the consequences of unleashing your inner jerk?

Great! Because Patch 7 releases on PC, today! And with it come new evil ending cinematics, along with Honour Mode improvements and new Legendary Actions, split screen improvements, a new way to mod your game, and a whole bunch of gameplay improvements and bug fixes.

Mac and console players, this is one of those patches that is so packed with changes and new features - including official modding support for all platforms - that it’s going to take a little longer to get this patch through all the necessary technical checks and requirements and into your hands. Although later than we originally expected, Patch 7 is headed to console and Mac in October, and we will keep you updated with our progress! 

Unfortunately, this does mean that console players will not be able to load cross-saves if they come from Patch 7 on PC - and multiplayer between PC and Mac will not be possible. We are still working on bringing crossplay to Baldur’s Gate 3, and like Patch 7, this requires a lot of work and testing before we're prepared to release it into the wild. 

We’ve still got a few more patches up our sleeve for Baldur’s Gate 3 - which will include both crossplay and photo mode, alongside other fixes and updates. But eventually all stories must come to an end. As Swen said during last week’s PAX West panel in Seattle - our final live panel for Baldur’s Gate 3 - it’s time for the team to go back to our cave and hang the armour on the wall while we focus on bringing you our next project.

In case you missed it, you can catch up on the panel here for a fond look-back at the making of Baldur’s Gate 3, as well as answers to some of your most infernally burning questions.

Patch 7 is certainly a big ‘un, and we’ve been busy tackling feedback and game bugs thanks to the help of mod authors who’ve been testing and populating the modding hub, as well as players who have been sharing their experience with Patch 7 during the Closed Beta. Thank you to all of you who had the opportunity to take part. The playtest has now ended and we’ll be taking this experience and carrying learnings from it into the future!

Patch 7 is approximately 11.6GB on PC, and will require 160GB of free space to install. If you find yourself without the space to install the update, we recommend uninstalling Baldur’s Gate 3 and then re-downloading the patched version!

As with any patch, some third-party mods may still become incompatible after our latest update. Please try uninstalling your mods and confirm whether the issue persists without them installed. If you continue to have issues after uninstalling all mods, do reach out to our support team. Please also remember to be patient with mod authors as they make any relevant adjustments to their mods!

We know many third-party mods utilise Script Extender, and as part of the Toolkit and patch testing with mod authors, efforts to help support compatibility with Patch 7 should mean that mods that require Script Extender will continue to work.

A big thank you to Norbyte, creator of Script Extender, and to all of the mod authors who have contributed to the Toolkit with their feedback! We couldn’t have done it without you.

And with that, let’s take a look at this thing!

Does Corruption Call Your Name?

The Sword Coast is yours to command, to rule like no other.

Whether you embraced absolute power, carried out your father’s will, played as an Origin character or were generally a menace to society, you’ll find Patch 7 now introduces 13 new cinematics that offer varying conclusions to your most evil playthroughs.

If you’re a streamer who is very demure, very mindful, and you use the 'Show Cinematic Nudity' option in the game's settings, it’s worth noting that we’ve now renamed this option to 'Show Sexual and Violent Cinematics' and updated its description to more accurately indicate what it does. This setting toggles explicit content plus a few select moments of extreme violence that may be distressing to some. We might have also embraced corruption a little too much because the new evil ending cinematics have been included in this setting. They really are that evil.

This setting does not affect your adventure, your choices, or your access to romance options; however, it does block sexual content with nudity and particularly violent scenes with gore.

Well, she got her dragon. But at what cost?

Whether you’re starting a new game or loading an old save to relive your battle with the Netherbrain, you’ll get to see these new cinematics depending on the choices you make.

It’s a One-Night Kinda Thing

Patch 7 & Modding Information

Looking to revisit the latest patch notes or want to try your hand at modding?
Check out the links below!

- Find the full patch notes for Patch 7 here.

- Hotfix #27 now live on all platforms.

- Get started with modding by following this guide.

Playing With Baldur’s Gate 3 Mods

If you’re thinking about starting a modded run and want to know what you’re getting into, whether you’re playing on console, Mac, or PC, then this is the guide for you!

Where do I even start?

So you want to enhance your journey to Baldur’s Gate with a little community-made magic? 

While the Baldur’s Gate 3 Toolkit used to create mods is only available on PC, a whole selection of player-created mods are now available on console and Mac! 

How are mods chosen for release on other platforms?

Only mods made with and uploaded using the Baldur’s Gate 3 Toolkit and which pass internal testing can be eligible for release on the console and Mac in-game mod browser. 

Technical limitations on certain platforms mean that some PC mods will not be available for Mac or console. Our team will need to test all mods requested to be brought to these platforms to confirm whether they can be made available. 

Mod Authors can let us know if they’d like to see their mod available on console and Mac during the upload process. Our Community Team will then check whether the mod adheres to our modding guidelines, before sending over batches of mods to undergo internal checks that look at the mod’s basic functionality, usability, and stability.

If all looks good, the mods will then be made available on these platforms! 

Will more mods be made available on console and Mac?

Yes! There are currently, uh, 69 mods that have passed internal testing, and we’ll be adding more as we go. Making mods available on platforms other than PC will be a continuously reviewed process that may change to include additional functionality in the future. Mods ready for both Mac and console that have passed testing will be released in batches, so keep an eye out on your in-game mod browser to see when new mods are added.

Please note: Not all PC mods will make it to consoles or Mac, and we kindly ask that you do not build upon an existing mod or port another mod author’s mods in an attempt to make them available in the in-game mod manager. 

Mod authors work hard to create their mods, whether they upload them via our Toolkit or third-party sites. Please respect their time and work!

To read up on what mods you can expect for console and Mac, please click here!

Navigating The In-Game Mod Manager

Browsing Mods In-Game 

- Discover mods by heading to the in-game Mod Manager when you start the game!

- On the Browse tab, use the filters to browse through a range of different mods.

- Please read the mod Description carefully. You may need to take additional steps for the mod to work correctly, such as downloading a separate mod or adjusting in-game settings.

- Hit the download button to install a mod, wait for it to download, and get ready to play!

Managing Your Mods

- Head to the Installed tab to view your installed mods.

- Disable or enable mods by checking the box to the right of the mod.

- Disabling some mods might affect your existing saves, so it’s a good idea to keep this in mind when you install mods!

Synchronising Mods

Whether you’re loading a modded savegame or planning on playing Multiplayer with your mods enabled, you’ll need the same version of mods installed. 

Say hello to the Verification Window! This window is designed to give you all the information and opportunity to synchronise the mods you currently have installed/enabled to the savegame or multiplayer game that you’re trying to join. 

When loading a savegame from either the main menu or when joining a Multiplayer session through direct connect from the lobby or by selecting a server, this window will be triggered.

Support Guide: How to enable Direct Connections.

When the Verification Window is shown, you might be presented with a few different options, which we’ve detailed in the table below.

 

 Download
 You’ll see the option to download a mod if you don’t already have it installed, but the Multiplayer session or savegame has that mod enabled.
 

 

 Enable
 If you don’t have a mod currently enabled, but the Multiplayer session does, you’ll see the option to enable it.
 

 

 Update
 You’ll see the option to update a mod if you have the mod enabled, but the Multiplayer session has a newer version.
 

 

 Downgrade
 You’ll see the option to downgrade a mod if you have the mod enabled, but the Multiplayer session has an older version.
 

 

 New Mods
 Mods listed under New Mods are ones that you have enabled but are not enabled in the Multiplayer session you are joining.
 

 

 Third-Party
 Mods listed as Third-party are mods that are not available via the in-game mod browser.
 

Cross-saves and Patch 7

With Patch 7 now rolling out to Mac and console players, cross-saves will once again be compatible. If you have PC saves that include curated mods (mods that have been approved for console or Mac), these should now work on your platform, and you will be prompted to download these mods when you try to use a cross-save on another platform.

If you have been playing with mods on PC that were not approved for console, the cross-save using these mods cannot be loaded on console.

Platform-based Achievements

Achievements are automatically disabled when you’re using mods, so keep this in mind if you’re still planning on completing your Baldur’s Gate 3 achievements! 

Troubleshooting Mods

When you download and play with files that modify your game, you change the way your game behaves, which can create conflicts with the way your game is designed to run. 

While console mods undergo basic stability testing, they are community-made, and changes to the game, such as a new update or mods with certain dependencies or conflicts, can impact how your mods function. 

Playing with a modded save sometimes means that issues can occur, such as:

- Failing to load past a certain percentage when starting a save

- Crashing on launch 

- Issues with the UI, including missing options or overlapping menus

- Shader issues, including missing makeup or face textures

- A land of naked avatars during Character Creation

If you run into an issue while using mods, you can help our support team track bugs by identifying whether the problem is with the game itself or a mod you may have installed. Understanding the distinction means we can offer you better official game support. However, we are unable to directly manage or fix any community-created mods.

Reporting Supported Mods: If you’ve noticed a mod that violates our guidelines, you can report it using the reporting functionality on the mod listing.

Try these steps:

- Navigate to the in-game Mod Manager and un-check your installed mods. With the mods disabled, see if the issue persists.

- If the issue no longer persists, and therefore seems related to a particular mod, you can reach out to the mod author and leave them a comment on the mod listing that explains some more about the issue you’re experiencing.

- If the issue persists without the mod installed and you believe the issue is with the base game, please report it to our support team using this report form.

Please note: If you are using third-party mods on PC, uninstalling and reinstalling the game will not remove all mod files. Please follow the steps outlined here to remove third-party mods!

Mods To Get You Started

Patch 7 releases on console with more than 60 community-made mods available and ready to download! Here are some of our favourites to get you started.

Adjustable Party Limit by PixellBytes

I will say that I have given this game more than its fair shake before posting this review.  My initial reaction when the game went to 1.0 last year was not a positive one.  Yet, with all the undying praise of this game and my enjoyment of this genre, I believed I had missed something that others had discovered.  I wanted to know what that was.  So over the past year I have started, stopped, uninstalled, reinstalled, and repeated this process numerous times.  I had made over half a dozen characters and new starts and only just in this recent play through finally was able to pull myself through Act 1.

I do not like this game.

It is final.  68 hours is more than enough.

[u][b]Presentation[/b][/u]

Let me get some praise out of the way before I get to the negatives.  Firstly, this game is beautiful.  The production values are top notch.  This is by far and away the most visually appealing cRPG I've ever played.  

In terms of sound outside of voice work, it is mostly passable.

[u][b]Story[/b][/u]

Here it comes, the bad.  

I do not think this is a good story.  

Not only is the story itself not good, the way it is told is downright awful.  It is disjointed and requires you to play through in a specific way to see it told in a coherent fashion.  This is a large failing because this game prides itself on being open-ended (not exactly [i]open[/i] world) and playing through the game organically (you know, actually [i]roleplaying[/i]) can lead to some truly bizarre instances where characters suddenly do or know something that did not happen in your playthrough.  

The biggest failing with the story is not that it is just poorly told, it is poorly conceived.  The main story is a bull rush of urgency.  You and your "friends" are not only dying, you're turning into a hive-mind tentacle monster that will torture you in unimaginable agony for days beforehand.  This is what we call, an [u]emergency[/u].  [i]Everything[/i] else should be not just secondary, but completely out of mind.  Does that matter?  No.  Quite the opposite, the game actively pushes you to do side content in order to progress in this silliness.

I'm old enough to remember people lambasting Fallout 4 for a similar main quest that completely eclipsed the rest of the side content.  Why was that awful and stupid and this is award-winning fiction?

Also, the setting is D&D Epic, but with low level mooks.  Epic settings lead to boring, uninspired, stories.  Mask of the Betrayer for NWN2 is a rare exception.

But hey, at least the characters are fun, right?

[u][b]Characters[/b][/u]

No, they are not.

I do not like these people that call themselves companions.  They are annoying.  They are poorly written, they are out of place, and in some cases, they are hilarious in the conception.

Take Wyll, for instance.  He is a chaotic good warlock that fancies himself the "Blade of Frontiers", a do-gooder that is willing to do anything for the greater good.  He has slain demons, minotaurs, devils, and assorted other fiends.  [i]By the dozens.[/i]  You meet him and he is level 2.

Alright Brenil, but the brain worms de-leveled him by 18!

Mhmm...  let me tell you a little something I learned from my experiencing DMing D&D.  Characters that have epic backstories, especially at level 1, are garbagemen.  They're terrible characters, usually Mary/Marty Sues that every one else hates and wishes would meet the gravedirt.

Okay, forget Wyll.  What about the others?  Oh, they're better.  But not much.  Astarion, Lae'zel, Karlach, and to some extent Gale, are all dumb and unlikable.  I'll give Gale a pass as he's supposed to be kind of a good-hearted goofball.  Astarion?  Edgy neutral evil vampire that belongs more in Twilight than D&D?  No.  Told him to go join the boar in the bush.  Lae'zel?  I gave her a try.  She played the lawful evil Githyanki quite well.  Too bad no one likes githyanki for a reason.  I told her to get in the brain machine in the creche and was disappointed with the semi-positive results.  Karlach?  See Wyll.

That leaves Minthara, Halsin, and Shadowheart.  Halsin?  Didn't interact much outside the story.  Shadowheart?  She's the most interesting companion you meet initially in Act 1, but she's a Cleric of Shar.  In Faerun, that usually means kill on sight.  Not exactly something you should [i]emblazon[/i] on your armor.  Unraveling her story is mildly interesting but nothing stellar.  I imagine her main appeal is that she is the most physically attractive character.

Last is not a companion you can recruit in Act 1, but she can become one later.  That is Minthara.  I actually enjoyed this character the most.  After choosing to side with her, you learn more about her and I actually cared to do so for the first time in the game.  Of course, siding with her means you do some dirty deeds, but by this point in my playing this game, I hated everyone anyway.

All that said, on the whole, the characters do not help the story.

But hey, Brenil, my man.  At least the game is fun, right?

[u][i]Gameplay[/i][/u]

No, it isn't.

BG3 uses 5th Edition D&D.  I am not a fan of 5th Edition, but I knew what I was getting into and I loved Solasta.  

The game is unfun to play.  The chief reason for this is two-fold.  

First, the UI.  The UI does nothing helpful for the player.  Finding out why X or Y enemies do Z is difficult and, sometimes, impossible to do in the game.  Like so much of the game, you have to look to an external source to help with a solution the UI should readily provide.  Add to this the awful inventory system that has learned [i]nothing[/i] from previous cRPGs, and you have poor inactive gameplay.

The active gameplay is the second problem.

This game has the worst encounters I have played in any cRPG in my life.  I have played a few of them.

The issue with the encounters in this game is that Larian thinks combat should be "challenging".  That's fine, I understand.  But challenging doesn't mean punishing.

Throughout Act 1 after the encounter at the Druid grove, the game decides to get cheeky.  Not just set pieces and boss fights.  [i]Every[/i] encounter.  Combat in this game is a puzzle.  The solution, more often than not, is metagaming, exploiting, save scumming, or all three.

To say this makes the game frustrating is an understatement.  Does it make it hard?  I suppose, but the solution is usually readily apparent - if you are willing to game the system right back.  But wait, isn't this a [i]roleplaying[/i] game?  Isn't meta knowledge an anathema to playing the role of a character?  No, shut up n00b, and sneak a barrel into the enemy camp and watch go boom.

Combat in this game is very similar to another cRPG series.  Divinity:  Original Sin.  I did not like those games either.  They were serious/silly RPGs that had bizarre mechanics and a huge emphasis on big explosions equals big fun.

[u][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/u]

Look, I have been harsh in this review.  I understand this.  I have been accused of being a contrarian.

I gave this game more than a fair chance to wow me.  The game actively frustrated me to the point of anger at times.  If a game is not fun.  Why play it?

I have seen other negative reviews here that follow my thought pattern.  Most will wave their hand and say something along the lines of, "It's a good game, its just not for me."  I disagree.  I believe this [i]is[/i] a bad game.  For what is a bad game if not one that gives you nothing but grief?  It can have well-made aspects, but the whole is greater than the parts and Baldur's Gate 3 is not worth your time or money.

Hmm... wait a moment.  I just remembered.  I didn't like The Witcher 3 either.  Crap.  Maybe I am just a contrarian after all.

I wish I could give an on the fence rating, as this game truly is extremely impressive. But I just want to put this out there for anyone who might be like me.
I went into this game having heard tales of its dedication to immersion, how every choice mattered, even the small ones. Maybe this set my expectations too high, maybe I was unlucky, but I can confidently say that, at least in my playthrough, this was not the case, at all.

Fundamentally, the moment-to-moment dialogue writing is just mediocre. There are memorable and charming characters, but, once you reach past the surface level, nearly every character has the most predictable, bog-standard reaction to every single situation they come across. Very rarely did any of the writing wow me with wit, expression, or character. It doesn't matter what happens, from simple banter to life-changing moments to deaths of loved ones, everything feels like a bland first draft you’d jot down before actually thinking of an interesting or moving way of writing a scene. Dialogue options are very obvious with what interactions they are trying to pull you into, sometimes even presupposing actions that make no sense for anyone involved (knowledge they could not possibly have, or referencing things I never did).
This lack of quality sadly extends to the story as a whole. I simply think Larian bit off more than they could chew, as the sheer scope of what they pulled off is unbelievably impressive, but still just not enough for what they were trying to do. Rather than even “just” a 100 hour game with tighter writing and more fleshed out characters, the game is ballooned to such a scale that few things feel fully finished and it leaves the entire experience feeling messy and hollow to me. There are a handful of key character progression points, but beyond those, I rarely had any meaningful connection to my party members. At the end of Act 1, the game suddenly shovels all their character moments on you in quick succession before pulling back again for most of Act 2. Fair enough, we’re in the thick of a dramatic plot, but the generic cultist villains just aren’t nearly as interesting.
I fully intended to finish the game despite my gripes, but the moment that finally broke me was this one (kept vague for spoiler reasons):
I was going through a dungeon that was important to one of my party members. They were raving about an ideology that I did not agree with, but every time the game gave me the ability to talk to them about it, the options boiled down to “Your ideology is fucking dumb” and “Yeah, you’re good C:”
I kept hoping to reach a point where the game would let me genuinely interact with their ideology and their character, but it never happened. I’ve heard there was some flag I could have set beforehand that would have made this character more amiable in this section, but that doesn’t fix my issue. In fact, it makes it worse, confining meaningful character interactions to whether you’ve completed a set scripted quest item is the opposite of immersive (except, it likely wouldn’t have been meaningful. i have reason to believe it would have been just as boring, but the character would have been easier to convince). By the end of the dungeon we reached a major decision point for this character, one that would further cement their ideology or let them break free from it. And once more, I was faced with essentially two options. “Don’t do it, I believe in you :,C” or “Yeah, you’re good C:” I then failed a persuasion check, the character turned hostile, and I was forced to kill them. This is all extremely disappointingly bland, but I could have lived with it.
However. The entire section had no further dialogue at all. Not from any of the other party members, not during the combat sequence, nothing. When I returned to camp afterwards, not a single one of the others had anything to say about the fact that we were just forced to tragically kill one of our friends and compatriots. Not a word of acknowledgment. I realized in that moment that Larian probably didn’t intend for anyone to actually go through with this story beat. Whether they lacked the time or the resources or whatever, I assume they figured players would just reload. Well I hadn’t reloaded once to change story outcomes in the 100 or so hours I had put in because I trusted the game to respect the choices I made. And what’s the point of having die-roll fail cases if I’m not actually meant to go through with them? I’d seen other character deaths go unacknowledged before (like an entire village’s worth of named characters being eradicated. nobody gave a shit. again, probably just figured the players would reload), but not a party member’s. That was one step too far and right then what was left of the immersion I had in this story completely shattered.
If you want a videogamey romp through a DnD world, you’ll have a good time. And that is a statement fully without judgment. I had a lot of fun with the combat and exploring the various locations is exciting and rewarding as a massive semi-open-world encounter-filled funhouse.
But if you want to be genuinely immersed in the story and characters and feel like your actions are meaningfully impactful, be prepared to potentially be game-ruiningly disappointed depending on what choices you make and how willing you are to look past the gaping holes left in the decision tree.

Minor grrr to end off:
The UI is straight up baffling. Randomly, things just won't stack, like you'll have 6 of an item and then just another stack of 2 more identical ones. Sometimes you can then manually stack them, sometimes the game just refuses. You can only send things to camp sometimes. Sometimes you can't mark and send multiple things to other characters or camp. Micromanaging your characters' inventories is a nightmare, especially in combat. Sometimes you can split a stack of potions to send to another party member, sometimes you just can't. I think this all has something to do with whether you’re sending from your main character, I honestly don't remember because it makes so little sense I probably compartmentalized the trauma.

As a long-time fan of the Baldur’s Gate series, I came into Baldur’s Gate 3 with high hopes, especially after seeing the overwhelmingly positive feedback. Unfortunately, after spending a few hours in the game, I find myself more frustrated than impressed.

Visually, the game is undeniably vibrant—perhaps too vibrant. The dark, gritty atmosphere that defined the earlier entries has been replaced with an overly colorful, almost cartoonish palette that feels out of place in the world of Baldur’s Gate. Instead of a deep and immersive fantasy world, it often feels like a whimsical reimagining, closer in style to Divinity: Original Sin than a continuation of the series I loved.

The writing is where the game really falters for me. Too often, the dialogue feels shallow, at times even cringe-inducing, lacking the depth and sophistication that made Baldur’s Gate 1&2 so engrossing. Rather than mature, nuanced storytelling, it sometimes feels like the game is trying too hard to cater to a broader, less demanding audience. It’s hard to connect with characters or take the plot seriously when the tone shifts awkwardly between campy humor and moments that should carry emotional weight but end up falling flat.

Mechanically, Baldur’s Gate 3 stays true to its D&D roots, and while that’s something I appreciate, it’s the overall tone and approach that make the game feel like it’s lost its way. The charm and complexity of the originals have been overshadowed by a focus on flashy visuals and quirky moments that often lack substance.

However, maybe it’s not entirely the game’s fault. Perhaps it’s a reflection of how times have changed. I’ve grown older, and the gaming landscape has evolved. It feels like we live in an era where entertainment leans toward simplicity, and audiences are more content with surface-level experiences. What once felt rich and complex has now given way to what some might call a more “accessible” approach. Sometimes, it feels like we’re living in a version of Idiocracy, where depth is sacrificed for instant gratification, and people celebrate what used to be considered basic.

In the end, Baldur’s Gate 3 may not be for everyone, especially those of us who grew up with the original games. It may resonate more with today’s players, but for me, it just doesn’t capture the magic that made the earlier entries so unforgettable.

Baldur’s Gate 3 Review: A Masterpiece of Immersion and World-Building

Baldur’s Gate 3, developed by Larian Studios, stands as a true triumph in the RPG genre, bringing to life the rich, complex world of Dungeons & Dragons like never before. Every element of the game is meticulously crafted to create an experience that is not only expansive but deeply immersive.

From the moment you start, you’re thrust into a world where your choices genuinely shape the narrative. The game’s branching storylines and intricate character interactions make you feel like an active participant rather than a passive observer. Every dialogue option, moral decision, and combat choice influences not just how NPCs respond but also the broader world around you. Whether you play as a noble hero or a morally gray adventurer, the consequences are tangible and often surprising, enhancing the feeling of being in a living, breathing world.

The character creation system is robust, with countless customization options that allow players to create unique personas. Each class, race, and background comes with its own set of abilities, proficiencies, and dialogue options, making every playthrough feel different. The game’s alignment with the D&D 5th Edition ruleset adds authenticity, giving roleplaying enthusiasts a genuine tabletop experience. Your character’s personality and background influence how they interact with other characters, adding depth to conversations and character arcs.

Visually, Baldur’s Gate 3 is a masterpiece. The environments are vibrant and detailed, with everything from dense forests to eerie, ancient ruins brought to life with stunning graphics and atmospheric lighting. The attention to detail is remarkable; even small elements like weather changes, flickering torchlight in dark dungeons, and the textures of characters’ clothing contribute to the immersive atmosphere. The cinematics, powered by motion capture, add another layer of realism, making characters’ expressions and movements feel incredibly lifelike. 

The turn-based combat system is intricate, strategic, and rewarding. It captures the essence of tabletop combat, with each encounter feeling like a puzzle to be solved. You can approach combat situations in multiple ways, whether it’s through brute force, stealth, or clever use of spells and terrain. Exploration is equally rich, with secret areas, hidden quests, and interactive objects scattered throughout the world. The game encourages curiosity, rewarding players who take the time to explore and experiment.

The audio design is another standout feature, amplifying the game’s immersive quality. From the sounds of weapons clashing in battle to the soft rustling of leaves during exploration, everything sounds authentic. The orchestral score, filled with dramatic highs and emotional lows, perfectly complements the game’s epic scale and intimate moments, drawing players even deeper into the world.

Final Thoughts

Baldur’s Gate 3 isn’t just a game; it’s an experience. It’s a testament to the power of storytelling and world-building, setting a new standard for immersive RPGs. Whether you’re a D&D veteran or new to the genre, Baldur’s Gate 3 offers a beautifully crafted adventure that is bound to captivate your imagination and leave a lasting impression.
